name: Nail wraps

card.summary: Pre-made adhesive nail coverings that give polished, designed nails without salon polish or acrylics.
card.note: Adhesives and nail cosmetics can cause allergic contact dermatitis in some people.

quick.overview:
Nail wraps are pre-designed adhesive coverings applied to the nail. They deliver a finished manicure look quickly, in many colours and patterns, and can be applied over existing polish or artificial nails.

Their appearance payoff is neat, groomed-looking hands without drying time or a salon visit. Dermatology literature mentions wraps as an option for people who want nail strengthening or have reactions to other nail products.
quick.how: The wrap is fitted to the nail, pressed on and trimmed, then removed later. They are used as a lower-commitment alternative to gel or acrylic.
quick.risks: Adhesives, including cyanoacrylate, can sensitise some users and cause eczema-like reactions around the nails. A hospital outbreak study also identified artificial nails or wraps as a risk factor for bacteria on health-care workers' hands.

lead: Nail wraps are pre-made designs that stick to the nail, offering a quick way to get nail art and usable over polish or acrylic nails.[1] They are grouped with press-ons and nail stickers among artificial nail options.[1]

They help appearance by giving hands a groomed, styled look with little application skill. A dermatology review notes that nail wraps or preformed nails can be applied where strengthening is the aim for people not sensitive to cyanoacrylate.[2]

angle.text: Wraps give finished-looking nails without drying time or salon tools, and some people use them to cover brittle or damaged nails.

paras: A review of contact sensitisation in nail cosmetics reports that acrylate and methacrylate monomers, formaldehyde and related resins can cause allergic dermatitis, and that even cyanoacrylate adhesives have been found allergenic, though they do not cross-react with acrylates.[2] Rashes may spread to the face and neck via contact transfer.[2]
In an investigation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a neonatal unit, a history of artificial nails or nail wraps was associated with colonisation of health-care workers' hands.[3]
No studies found on nail wraps as a cosmetic treatment; related safety research on nail cosmetics is described above.[2][3]
